interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through how KMP achieves O(n+m) substring search when brute force is O(n·m).
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The gap comes from what happens on a mismatch. Brute force, after matching some prefix of the pattern and then failing, throws all of that progress away and restarts comparison one position to the right — on a text like `"aaaaaaaaab"` searching for `"aaab"`, that means re-matching 3 characters over and over at nearly every position, which is where the O(n·m) worst case actually comes from.

KMP refuses to discard that information. Before scanning, it precomputes the **LPS array** from the pattern alone: `lps[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that's also a proper suffix of it. That array answers, for any partial match, "what prefix of the pattern is already guaranteed to be sitting in the text right now?"

During the scan, a mismatch after matching `j` characters doesn't restart — it falls back to `j = lps[j-1]` and retries at the *same* text position. The text pointer `i` never moves backward, which is the invariant that bounds total text comparisons to O(n). Building the LPS array itself is O(m), using the same self-referential fallback trick on the pattern against itself.

So the full picture is O(m) to build the array plus O(n) to scan, giving O(n+m) — and unlike brute force, that bound holds for every input, not just typical ones.

**Testing:** whether you understand LPS as reused progress information, not just a memorized array to precompute.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: What exactly does lps[i] represent, and why is 'proper' prefix/suffix important in that definition?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
`lps[i]` is the length of the longest string that is simultaneously a **proper prefix** and a **proper suffix** of `pattern[0..i]`. Proper means strictly shorter than the substring itself — the whole substring trivially matches itself as both prefix and suffix, so excluding that case is what makes the value meaningful.

Concretely, for `pattern = "ababaca"`, look at `pattern[0..3] = "abab"`. Its proper prefixes are `"a", "ab", "aba"`; its proper suffixes are `"b", "ab", "bab"`. The longest string appearing in both lists is `"ab"`, length 2 — so `lps[3] = 2`.

Why this matters for the algorithm: when a match fails partway through the pattern, the text already contains — verified, no need to re-check — a copy of whatever prefix of the pattern you'd matched so far. If that matched prefix has a shorter piece that's also a suffix of itself, that shorter piece is *also* still sitting in the text right where you are, ready to serve as the start of a new match attempt without moving the text pointer back. Drop the "proper" restriction and `lps[i]` would just equal `i+1` for every position, which encodes zero information — you'd never be able to fall back to anything shorter than what you already had.

**Testing:** whether you can derive the definition's purpose rather than reciting "longest prefix suffix" as a slogan.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Would you actually use a hand-rolled KMP implementation in production code, or reach for something else?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
In application code, no — I'd reach for the language's built-in string search (`str.find`, `strstr`, `String.indexOf`), because those are typically tuned hybrids (often Boyer-Moore-ish skip tables or SIMD-accelerated substring scans) that outperform a textbook KMP on typical, non-adversarial text, and they've had years of edge-case hardening I'm not going to match by hand.

Where I'd specifically reach for KMP, or at least its guarantee, is when the input is adversarial or the worst case is a real risk rather than a theoretical one: scanning untrusted network payloads for a signature, or matching against text an attacker partially controls. Brute force's O(n·m) worst case isn't exotic — it's trivially triggerable with a repetitive pattern like `"aaa...ab"` against similarly repetitive text — and an attacker who knows you're using brute force can construct input specifically to burn CPU. KMP's O(n+m) bound holds regardless of input shape, which is the actual guarantee you're paying the extra LPS-array bookkeeping for.

The honest signal to give an interviewer: know when the guaranteed bound matters enough to hand-roll it, rather than defaulting to "I'd implement KMP" for every substring problem when the built-in would do.

**Testing:** whether you can weigh a guaranteed bound against a well-tuned average-case implementation, rather than treating KMP as always the "better" answer.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: Your KMP implementation passes on simple test strings but returns wrong match positions on a specific repetitive input. How would you debug it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The failure mode you describe — correct on simple cases, wrong on repetitive patterns — is the signature of an off-by-one in the LPS fallback, so that's where I'd look first rather than re-deriving the whole algorithm.

I'd isolate the LPS array construction from the main scan and print it standalone against a pattern chosen specifically to have internal repetition, like `"aabaabaa"`. I'd hand-trace the expected values (it should climb during the repeated `"aab"` stretches and reset sharply at breaks) and compare against the printed output — a mismatch here means the bug is in `build_lps`, most likely the fallback using `lps[length]` instead of `lps[length - 1]`, or resetting `length` to 0 on a mismatch instead of falling back through the array.

If the LPS array itself checks out, I'd move to the main scan and check the two places it also uses `lps`: the mismatch fallback (`j = lps[j-1]`) and, easy to miss, the **post-match** fallback — after recording a full match, the code should still fall back to `lps[j-1]` rather than resetting `j` to 0, otherwise overlapping matches (like `"aa"` inside `"aaa"` at both position 0 and 1) get silently dropped.

The reason simple test strings pass despite this bug: without internal repetition, the fallback path is barely exercised, so a wrong index only shows up once the pattern has real structure to fall back through — which is exactly why the fix is to test with repetitive patterns from the start, not as an afterthought.

**Testing:** whether you can localize a subtle correctness bug to the specific line pattern that causes it, rather than re-deriving KMP from scratch under pressure.
